source_text:
ἄνθρωπος οὗτος ὡς θεὸς τὸν θάνατον ἐσκύ λευσεν. Πάλιν ὡς νεκρὸν οἱ στρατιῶται
ἐφρούρησαν καὶ ὡς θεὸν οἱ πυλωροὶ τοῦ ᾅδου θεωρήσαντες ἔπτηξαν.
3 Τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον ἐρεῖς, οὐκ ἄλλον καὶ ἄλλον, οὐδὲ ἄλλον ἐν
ἄλλῳ, οὐδὲ ἄλλον δι' ἄλλου· εἷς γὰρ ὢν ὁ σαρκω θεὶς Λόγος εἰς ἓν ταῦτα κἀκεῖνα ὡς
ἠβουλήθη ἀρρήτῳ λόγῳ συνήγαγεν· καὶ τὴν μὲν σάρκα διακονῆσαι τοῖς πάθεσι
δέδωκεν, τῇ θεότητι δὲ πρὸς τὰ σημεῖα καὶ τὰ θαύματα κέχρηται, ἀλλ' ὥσπερ οὐ
θεμιτὸν τὸν Λόγον ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς χωρίζεσθαι, οὕτως ἀνάγκη τὰ παθήματα
συμπεπλέχθαι τοῖς θαύμασιν.
thought_title: The one incarnate Word suffers in flesh and works miracles in divinity, inseparably woven
orientation: Hesychius continues showing how Jesus was treated as dead by human actors but revealed as God by divine power, insisting these are not two persons but the single incarnate Word whose sufferings and miracles are inextricably interwoven.
pass_a_gloss: This man as God despoiled death. Again as a dead man the soldiers guarded him, and as God the gatekeepers of Hades seeing him trembled in fear. You will say the same one is also that one, not another and another, nor another in another, nor another through another; for being one the incarnate Word gathered these things and those things into one as he willed by an ineffable word; and he gave the flesh to serve the sufferings, but he used the divinity for the signs and the miracles, but just as it is not permissible for the Word to be separated from the flesh, so it is necessary for the sufferings to be interwoven with the miracles.

choices.why: Glossary sense 'incorruptibility' is the result; here Christ actively strips death of its spoils, matching the verb's force of plundering a defeated enemy.
The prefix συν- plus ἄγω means to bring together into unity; the incarnate Word unifies the human and divine actions in one person.
Perfect passive infinitive of συμπλέκω; the sufferings and miracles are not merely joined but woven through each other, inseparable.
ἀρρήτῳ dative of instrument; the Word's own unutterable decree accomplishes the union, not a human explanation.
Repetition of ἄλλον denies any division into two persons; the homilist excludes Nestorian 'another and another' language.
rejected: not someone else and someone else

choices.why: Aorist active infinitive of διακονέω; the flesh is given as a servant to the sufferings, not as their master.

pass_b_english: This man despoiled death as God. Again the soldiers guarded him as a dead man, and the gatekeepers of Hades, seeing him as God, cowered in fear. You will say that he is the same one in both: the one who suffers and the one who works wonders. He is not one and another, not one person inside another, not one acting through another. For the incarnate Word, being one, gathered these things and those into one by an ineffable word, as he willed. He gave the flesh to serve the sufferings, and he employed his divinity for the signs and the miracles. But just as it is not right for the Word to be separated from the flesh, so the sufferings must be interwoven with the miracles.

problems.quote: You would call this same one that same one
problems.source_quote: Τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον ἐρεῖς
problems.why: The sense is that the same subject is both the man and God. The English reads as a puzzling tautology and hides the claim.
problems.fix: You will say that he is the same one in both: the one who suffers and the one who works wonders. He is not one and another.
problems.ruling: ἐρεῖς takes τὸν αὐτόν as predicate of τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον: call this one and that one the same person. English collapses the contrast into a tautology.

edits.old: You would call this same one that same one — not another and another, not one person inside another, not one acting through another.
edits.new: You will say that he is the same one in both: the one who suffers and the one who works wonders. He is not one and another, not one person inside another, not one acting through another.

fixed: Replaced the puzzling tautology 'You would call this same one that same one' with 'You will say that he is the same one in both: the one who suffers and the one who works wonders' to accurately reflect Τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον ἐρεῖς and the theological claim that the single incarnate Word is the subject of both sufferings and miracles.

last_rejected.quote: You will say that he is the same one in both: the one who suffers and the one who works wonders.
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον ἐρεῖς
last_rejected.why: τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον means this one and that one (the man guarded as dead and the one seen as God), not sufferer and wonder-worker.
last_rejected.fix: You will call this one and that one the same, not one and another, not one in another, not one through another.
last_rejected.ruling: Τὸν αὐτὸν δὲ τοῦτον κἀκεῖνον: 'this one and that one' are the man/sufferer and God/wonder-worker; the English's sufferer and wonder-worker reading matches context (παθήματα/θαύματα) and is a fair gloss.
